title: Langar on the highway
hook: in the farmers' protests of 2020 and 2021 langar fed protesters on the roads

segments.voice: Yesterday, explaining the turban, and your line was ask, then learn. Did you ask someone a real question? Today, a kitchen that refused to stay indoors. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

Tractors parked nose to tail along a highway, as far down the road as the eye can follow. Behind them, steam rising from huge pots. Somebody kneading dough on a tarp. Somebody flipping rotis on a wide iron griddle. A line of people sitting on the asphalt in a row, plates in their laps. Farmers had come to the edges of Delhi to protest new farm laws, and they camped there, on the roads, through heat and through cold. A camp that size needs feeding. Nobody set up a canteen with a cash register. They set up langar.
screen: `TRACTORS ALONG THE HIGHWAY.` → `POTS, DOUGH, A GRIDDLE.` → `NOT A CANTEEN. LANGAR.`

segments.voice: First, the camp. People held different views about the farm laws, and this lesson isn't here to settle that. It is here for the kitchen. Among the farmers on the roads were Sikhs from Punjab, and they brought what Sikhs bring when a crowd gathers: rations, cooks, and the habit of feeding anyone who sits down. Second, the root. Langar is the free kitchen of the Guru's house, and Sikh tradition traces it back to the Gurus themselves. In a hymn by the bards Satta and Balwand, at Ang 967 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the langar of the Guru runs on, and its stores never run short. The same hymn praises Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad, who served in the langar, giving out rich rice pudding made with ghee, and whose kindness gave wide shade. Langar, from the start, was a kitchen with names and hands. Third, the road. On the highway, langar did what it does in a gurdwara. It didn't check who you were. Farmers ate, and so did passersby, reporters, and people who simply lived nearby and walked over. Volunteers washed dishes on the roadside. Some kept pots going through the night. Fourth, the point. A gurdwara is a building, but langar was never really about the building. It is about the habit: where people gather, cook; where people are tired, feed them; and sit together, in a row, on the same ground. When the farmers moved onto the road, the kitchen didn't wait for them to come back. It came along.
screen: `DIFFERENT VIEWS. TODAY, THE KITCHEN.` · `ANG 967: STORES THAT NEVER RUN SHORT.` · `FARMERS, PASSERSBY, NEIGHBORS.` · `NOT THE BUILDING. THE HABIT.` · then, large: `THE KITCHEN CAME ALONG.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with someone tired. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person in your life who is worn out right now. A parent on night shifts. A friend in a hard month. A coworker carrying too much. See their face. Breathe in, and notice how tired they look. Breathe out, and ask yourself one plain question: what could I bring them to eat or drink this week? A meal, a coffee, a bag of fruit, a plate dropped at the door. Don't plan the whole thing. Just let one answer arrive. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Langar on the highway. When farmers camped on the roads, the Guru's free kitchen went with them and fed whoever sat down. Today's word.

Your line: the kitchen came along. Today, feed someone who's tired, even with something small, and bring it to where they are instead of waiting for them to come to you. Day one thousand twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs serve langar, a free communal meal, at gurdwaras, and volunteers often take it out to where people gather, at protests, disasters and long journeys.

trapdoor: what you thought: langar is the meal served inside a gurdwara.
what it means: a free kitchen that goes wherever people gather, even onto a highway, and feeds whoever sits down.
what a scholar hears: Satta and Balwand's hymn at Ang 967 already names the langar and Mata Khivi's service in it, so the kitchen sits inside the Guru Granth Sahib itself.
